Female Pit sculpin attain a maximum total length of 13 centimeters [Li = 13 centimeters], a value consistent with the modest body sizes typical of cottids occupying cool, headwater streams. This asymptotic size is reached after several years of growth, and the species displays the relatively slow, determinate growth pattern common among small-bodied benthic fishes in the Pacific Northwest. The ultimate wet weight for females reaches 21.7 grams [Wwi = 21.7 grams], a mass that reflects the robust, large-headed morphology characteristic of this genus. Specimens captured from the upper Sacramento River drainage during late summer surveys yielded gravid females approaching this upper size limit, suggesting that the local population achieves the full growth potential reported for the species. The relationship between length and weight in this species conforms closely to the general allometric pattern observed in congeneric sculpins, with females investing substantial somatic resources into the pronounced abdominal cavity needed for egg production.

Sexual maturation in female Pit sculpin occurs upon reaching a total length of 5 centimeters [Lp = 5 centimeters], a size typically attained during the second year of life. This length at puberty is relatively small compared to other members of the Cottus genus, reflecting the species' adaptation to cool, low-productivity environments where early maturation may confer a selective advantage. Field collections from mid-elevation California streams indicate that females measuring close to this threshold exhibit the first visible signs of ovarian development, including the onset of vitellogenesis. The synchrony between size and reproductive activation suggests that attainment of a minimum body length is a proximate cue for the initiation of gametogenesis, rather than age alone. This pattern of size-based puberty is widespread among freshwater cottids and is often linked to the energetic constraints imposed by seasonal food availability in montane habitats.

The reproductive output of Pit sculpin has been characterized under controlled laboratory conditions at a stable water temperature of 13 °C [T = 13 °C]. Females maintained at this temperature produce approximately 320 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = approximately 320 eggs per spawning event], with roughly one spawning event per year [F_R_i = roughly one spawning event per year]. This value was derived from continuous monitoring of captive breeding pairs over a full annual cycle, during which females exhibited a protracted spawning season. The rate of egg production is modest compared to more fecund temperate cottids, likely reflecting the species' relatively small body size and the energetic costs associated with producing comparatively large, yolky eggs. Spawning events were observed every several days, with females depositing adhesive eggs in a single layer on the underside of flat rocks within the stream substrate. The constant thermal regime used in these experiments approximates the mean summer water temperatures typical of the species' native range.

Neonatal Pit sculpin emerge from the egg with a wet weight at birth of 0.0083 grams [Wwb = 0.0083 grams], a value derived from the average egg diameter of 2.5 millimeters. This minute birth mass places the species among the smaller-bodied freshwater cottids and is consistent with the production of relatively large, yolk-rich eggs that sustain the prolarvae through the endotrophic phase prior to first feeding. The relationship between egg size and larval mass in this species follows the expected geometric scaling from a spherical egg of that diameter, assuming a density typical of teleost eggs. Upon hatching, the yolk-sac larvae remain adhesive and typically stay within the interstitial spaces of the gravel nest, where they absorb their yolk reserves over a period of several days. The small initial size of the newly emerged prolarvae imposes a narrow window for successful first feeding, as the mouth gape remains limited until the onset of exogenous nutrition.

Maximum documented lifespan in Pit sculpin reaches approximately 5.5 years [am = approximately 5.5 years] when individuals are maintained at a constant water temperature of 13 °C [T = 13 °C]. This longevity is relatively extended for a fish of such modest adult body size and aligns with the slow pace of life typical of cold-water benthic fishes inhabiting stable thermal environments. In natural populations, the oldest individuals are typically captured from deeper, thermally buffered pools where predation pressure is lower and seasonal temperature fluctuations are dampened. The combination of delayed maturity, modest fecundity, and extended lifespan positions this species as a classic K-selected strategist among the freshwater ichthyofauna of California. Senescence in aged individuals is typically marked by a gradual decline in body condition and a reduction in reproductive output during the final year of life.
